title: CERT-In Names 'Crafty Falcon' in AI Attacks on Indian Financial Firms
excerpt: The November 4 advisory names four AI tools — at least two linked by researchers to China — behind breaches at lenders, fintechs and crypto exchanges.
body:
• CERT-In's November 4 advisory names a group it calls "Crafty Falcon," which has breached Indian non-bank lenders, fintech firms and crypto exchanges using publicly available AI tools "at machine speed."
  • The advisory names four tools — ARTEX, PentAGI, Cairn and CyberStrikeAI; security researchers have linked at least two to China, and CrowdStrike says ARTEX has been used against South Korean banks since late September.
  • Attacks were timed to holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring windows, and firms that patched incompletely after earlier alerts were hit again.
  • CERT-In did not name affected companies, say how much was stolen, or attribute the campaign to any state; for diaspora readers, the practical risk sits with India-based lending and payment apps that move money through shared APIs.

India's cybersecurity agency CERT-In has named the hacking group behind a wave of AI-driven attacks on financial firms and identified the tools it uses, at least two of them linked by researchers to China, according to Reuters. The group, which CERT-In calls "Crafty Falcon," has breached non-bank lenders, fintech firms and cryptocurrency exchanges, the agency said in an advisory issued on Wednesday, November 4. CERT-In described the threat as "active and ongoing."

How the attacks work

CERT-In said the attackers use publicly available AI tools to automate break-ins "at machine speed." The group "surveys its targets with machine intelligence" and moves money by invoking the victims' own payment and disbursement systems — the same interfaces lenders and fintechs use to push loans and transfers to customers. The four tools named in the advisory are ARTEX, PentAGI, Cairn and CyberStrikeAI.

https://x.com/H4ckmanac/status/2118015902314578425

Timing is part of the method. Attacks were scheduled around holidays, weekends and other periods with fewer staff monitoring systems, delaying detection. Firms that had fixed flaws after earlier CERT-In alerts were attacked again where their remediation was incomplete.

What is — and is not — attributed

CERT-In did not say who is behind Crafty Falcon or where the group operates, and it did not describe the attacks as state-sponsored. The China connection runs through the tooling: researchers have linked at least two of the four tools to China, and cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike has said ARTEX, a tool made in China, has been used against banks in South Korea since late September, and by a China-linked group in an espionage campaign against more than 200 organisations in at least 14 countries. ARTEX's developer made the tool private last month after those allegations surfaced.

The incidents behind the warning

The advisory follows a spate of attacks on Indian banks and non-bank lenders in recent weeks, during which the Reserve Bank of India has tightened cybersecurity checks. Reuters, citing a police complaint, previously reported that two Mumbai-based non-banking lenders lost approximately $2 million through more than 700 unauthorised instant transfers on October 8 and 9, handled through ICICI Bank, after hackers broke into the APIs that banks, lenders and fintech firms use to communicate about payments and loan disbursement. In the same period, State Bank of India disclosed a leak of 3,897 customer records on the dark web, Spandana Sphoorty Financial reported unauthorised debits from a bank account on November 1, and AU Small Finance Bank said it was investigating a potential customer-data leak. CERT-In did not link specific incidents to Crafty Falcon.

What to watch

CERT-In, the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre and the IT ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. For financial firms, the advisory's practical message is completeness: partial patching after the October alerts is exactly what the group is exploiting, and low-staffing windows — the Diwali season included — are when it prefers to move.
